card.name: Pantsula
card.tagline: South Africa's township dance — born in 1950s Soweto under apartheid, footwork low and lightning, Dickies and bucket hats.
card.profile: Pantsula is a tradition and also a highly energetic dance form that originated in the black townships of South Africa during the apartheid era. It developed into a form of social commentary for black South Africans and has undergone several transformations with the country's changing political tides.
card.insight: After the end of apartheid in 1994, pantsula persisted as an expression of cultural roots for many black South Africans.
card.profile_long:
Pantsula emerged in the 1950s and 1960s within the townships of Alexandra and Sophiatown in Johannesburg. It began as a series of informal street dance competitions among older men, serving as a creative response to the forced removals implemented by the apartheid government. By the 1980s, the practice had expanded beyond its male-only origins to include black South Africans of all ages, becoming a powerful tool for political resistance and public awareness regarding social issues like AIDS. Following the end of apartheid in 1994, the dance persisted as a core element of cultural identity, eventually gaining popularity across diverse demographics in South Africa.

The technique of pantsula is defined by its syncopated, quick-stepping, and low-to-the-ground movement. It is a flat-footed dance that emphasizes the use of the limbs and a sense of exaggeration. Practitioners often train in groups for many hours each week to master the rigorous physical demands of the form. The dance is categorized into three primary styles: Western style, Slow poison, and Futhuza. Western style is the most common and rigorous, characterized by an upright torso with arms wrapped around the body, while the feet perform extremely fast, particular shuffling and jumping movements. Slow poison maintains the stationary arm position of the Western style but is performed in a slow, steady fashion with a constant beat. Futhuza incorporates elements of American hip-hop and breakdancing, utilizing the disjointed, robotic motions of popping and locking.

Historically, the music for pantsula was live, featuring voices such as Bra Sello and 'Big Voice Jack' Lerole. As technology evolved, dancers began to incorporate international pop music, including tracks by Michael Jackson, MC Hammer, and P Diddy. In the 1990s, a distinct genre known as kwaito emerged as the definitive soundtrack for the dance. Kwaito is a multilingual blend of seSotho, isiZulu, English, and Afrikaans, described as strong and sharp, projecting a streetwise, urban image. 

In contemporary culture, pantsula has gained international visibility through various media. It was featured in the 2018 music video for 'All the Stars' by Kendrick Lamar and showcased in the 2021 Netflix drama series 'Jiva!'. The dance is also the subject of the hyper-reality TV series 'Tjo Vitjo', which premiered in 2017. Furthermore, the 2015 song 'Makeba' by French singer-songwriter Jaine, which features pantsula dancers in its music video, saw a viral resurgence in 2023, further cementing the dance's place in the global digital landscape.

sections.origins_and_history: Pantsula emerged in the 1950s and 1960s in Alexandra and Sophiatown, Johannesburg, as a response to forced removals by the apartheid government. It began as informal street competitions among men before becoming a broader tool for political resistance and social awareness by the 1980s.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Pantsula is a flat-footed, low-to-the-ground dance. It features three styles: Western (fast shuffling and jumping with an upright torso), Slow poison (slow, steady, stationary arms), and Futhuza (incorporating popping and locking).
sections.music_and_instruments: Music has evolved from live performances by artists like Bra Sello and 'Big Voice Jack' Lerole to international pop and the 1990s genre kwaito, a multilingual blend of South African languages.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a form of street competition, it became a medium for social commentary, political resistance, and expressing cultural roots.
sections.notable_figures: Bra Sello, 'Big Voice Jack' Lerole, Vincent Moloi, Warren Masemola, Rapulana Seiphemo.
sections.lineage: Developed from Sotho dances of mqaquanga and marabi, with influences from 1930s American jazz, and later 1980s American hip-hop and breakdance.

claims.text: Pantsula dance emerged in the 1950s and 1960s as a response to the forced removals implemented by the apartheid government.
It began in Alexandra and Sophiatown, two townships in Johannesburg, as groups of older men engaged in informal street dance competitions.
Pantsula was used as an expression of resistance during the political struggle then occurring against the apartheid government.
Pantsula is a syncopated, quick-stepping, low to the ground form of dance which evokes the urban street culture of which it is a part of.
Pantsula has three styles: Western style, slow poison, and futhuza.
In the 1990s, a particular type of music for pantsula emerged: kwaito.

observation.levels_jumps_turns: Frequent jumps, high knee kicks, low crouches, and quick turns
